How to assess a senior engineer’s technical depth

A practical guide for HR leaders: how to assess a senior engineer’s technical depth and judgement when you can’t evaluate the work yourself.

  1. Home
  2. Insights
  3. How to assess a senior engineer’s technical depth

24 November 2026 · 5 min read

  • Guide
  • HR leaders

You are hiring a senior embedded software engineer, a security architect or a lead process engineer. The CVs look alike: the same tools, similar job titles, years of experience that all sound right. You can check motivation, communication and fit, but you can’t tell whether the person can actually do the work.

That gap is where most failed senior hires start. The good news is that you don’t need to become an engineer to close it. You need a process that puts technical judgement where it belongs and keeps everything else consistent.

Agree what “senior” means before the search starts

“Senior” means different things in different companies. In one it is a matter of years, in another it means owning a system end to end, mentoring others or talking to customers. If HR and the hiring manager don’t agree on it up front, every interview measures something different.

Before the role is advertised, ask the hiring manager three questions:

  • What will this person deliver in their first year? Three to five concrete outcomes, such as “take over the test bench software” or “lead the ISO 27001 audit preparation”.
  • Which competences are essential on day one, and which can they learn? Keep the essential list short. Every item on it should be something you can test.
  • What does this person decide alone? Seniority shows in the decisions someone is trusted with, not in the length of their tool list.

Write the answers down. They become the scorecard every interviewer uses.

Put an engineer in the process

Technical depth can only be judged by someone who knows the discipline. That might be a senior engineer from your own team, an external specialist, or a recruitment partner whose screening is run by engineers. What matters is that:

  • the technical interview follows a structure, with the same core questions for every candidate;
  • it tests the competences agreed in the brief, not the interviewer’s favourite topics;
  • the interviewer writes a short assessment, with evidence, before talking to anyone else about the candidate.

A written assessment protects you from the most common failure in technical hiring: one confident opinion in a debrief that nobody else can challenge.

What you can assess yourself

Not everything needs an engineer. Several signals of seniority are visible to anyone who listens carefully.

Can they explain their work to you? Senior engineers spend much of their time explaining trade-offs to managers, customers and colleagues from other teams. Ask them to describe the hardest problem in their last project as they would to a new colleague from another department. A clear, structured answer is a good sign. Jargon used to avoid the question is not.

Do they talk about decisions or only about tasks? Listen for “we chose”, “I recommended”, “I pushed back because”. Juniors describe what they did. Seniors also explain why, what the alternatives were, and what they would do differently now.

How do they talk about failure? Ask about a project that went wrong. You are looking for ownership and what they changed afterwards, not for a story where someone else was to blame.

What do they ask you? Strong senior candidates ask about the team, the technical debt, who makes decisions and what success looks like. Questions only about the package can mean the role is not their real interest.

Questions that reveal depth

These questions work in an HR interview and give the technical interviewer useful material:

  • “Tell me about a technical decision you would make differently today.”
  • “What did you stop doing yourself as you became more senior?”
  • “When did you disagree with your manager or a customer on a technical point, and what happened?”
  • “How do you get up to speed in a system or plant you don’t know?”
  • “Who learned the most from working with you, and what did you teach them?”

Write down the answers in the candidate’s own words. They are evidence you can compare across candidates, rather than an impression.

Signals to weigh carefully

Job titles. A “lead” in a small company may carry more responsibility than a “principal” in a large one, or much less. Ask what the person owned, not what they were called.

Tool lists. Listing a tool says little about how deeply someone knows it. The technical interview should probe two or three essential tools in depth rather than tick off ten.

Certifications. In some fields, such as cybersecurity or functional safety, certifications show a baseline of knowledge and may be required by clients. They don’t prove that someone can apply that knowledge on a real project.

Long take-home tasks. Senior people who are not actively looking rarely give up a weekend for an unpaid exercise. A structured discussion of a past project, or a short exercise done together in the interview, tells you more and keeps good candidates in the process.

Make the decision a joint one

Agree the roles before the interviews start. HR owns the process: the scorecard, the order of the steps, consistent questions, feedback to candidates and the timeline. The technical interviewer owns the judgement on technical competences. The hiring manager owns the final decision, based on both.

In the debrief, ask each interviewer to share their scores and evidence before the discussion starts. Disagreements are useful: they show where the evidence is thin and what to check in a final conversation or a reference.
